independence_scope: intra-mesh Anthropic-family; agreement is corroboration, never cross-provider evidence

reviews.reasoning: Span Ps.24.1-Ps.24.2 with a rear seam at 24:3. Re-derived rather than trusted: web_mt_offset_map.json records psalms.24 as rule 'identity' (web_verses 10 = mt_verses 10, mt_title_verses []), and psalm_device_inventory.json superscriptions.24 records mt_title_verses 'prefix_of_v1' with labels mizmor + le_david; the bytes agree, since oshb:Ps.24.1 opens לְדָוִ֗ד מִ֫זְמ֥וֹר before the cosmic-ownership clause. The row's title claim and its web:Ps.24.0 = oshb:Ps.24.1 form are therefore correct, and that form is owner-ruled for opening rows of titled psalms. Both WEB quotes are verbatim (check_web_quotes over the cluster: 25 quotes checked, 0 flags). The rear seam is carried by a tier-1 discourse-mode shift that I confirmed in the Hebrew: MT 24:3 opens with the interrogative מִֽי יַעֲלֶ֥ה, against the declarative predication of vv. 1-2, so the declarative-to-interrogative warrant is real and 'high' is calibrated. Selah: pmarks_Ps.json records selah in Ps 24 at Ps.24.6 and Ps.24.10 only, one occurrence each; the span carries none and the row claims none, so nothing is span-scoped wrongly. Two observations that do not rise to defects. First, the row's sole observed_substrate_signal, poetry_lines 1 at Ps.24.1 and Ps.24.2, has no discriminating power at the seam it is offered beside: verse_map_web gives poetry_lines 1 at Ps.24.3 as well, and WEB poetic lineation is modern formatting rather than a text signal. The row does not lean on it - the interrogative shift carries the seam - so the field is uninformative rather than wrong. Second, the row asserts an MT-internal fact (the title sitting inside MT v1) without quoting the title bytes; I do not file that, because the assertion is machine-checked against the designated arithmetic authority by the dual-cite ref the row does carry, and citation_sweep returns GREEN on it.

Span Ps.24.3-Ps.24.6. Both Hebrew quotes collate at byte tier against the refs they are cited to (collate.py: oshb:Ps.24.3 byte; oshb:Ps.24.6 byte), so both are quotation-grade. The K/Q handling is the strongest thing in this row and I checked it end to end: pmarks_Ps.json kq records exactly one note at Ps.24.6; the staged extract serializes ketiv and qere inline in the verse; the row quotes oshb:Ps.24.6 whole - hence both readings appear in its Hebrew - and then discloses which token is which, both collating at byte. No reading is selected, which is the correct treatment. Quote and gloss cover the same span in both witnesses (whole WEB verse against whole MT verse). Selah at Ps.24.6 verified in the inventory (1 occurrence), inside the span, and used only as a closural corroborator: the drivers are the interrogative frame opening at 24:3, which I confirmed in the bytes as מִֽי יַעֲלֶ֥ה, and the summarizing identification at 24:6. That keeps selah at corroboration strength, not driver strength. WEB 24:6 is reproduced verbatim including the capitalized pronoun and the em dash. Rear seam is sound: MT 24:7 opens the imperative gate-address, a different addressee and mood from the third-person qualifications of vv. 4-6. 'high' is calibrated for a seam pair this clean.

Span Ps.24.7-Ps.24.10 is right and I do not contest it: MT 24:7 opens an imperative address to the gates and 24:10 closes on selah, verified at Ps.24.10 in pmarks_Ps.json. Both Hebrew quotes collate byte, and both substrate sweeps are exactly correct as stated - I re-ran them: the three-word gate-command opening returns 2 verses / 2 occurrences book-wide (oshb:Ps.24.7, oshb:Ps.24.9), and the king-of-glory string returns 4 verses / 5 occurrences book-wide, all inside the span. The defect is that the prose claim exceeds the object those sweeps measured. The rationale says the gate command is 'repeated word-for-word' at 24:9, and the rejected_alternative rests its whole case against a 7-8 / 9-10 split on 'the word-for-word repetition of the gate-command line', attaching the 2-verse count to it. In the bytes the line is not repeated word-for-word at any tier: 24:7 and 24:9 are nine words each and two of the nine differ, including a change of binyan in the second imperative, which is a semantic difference and not an orthographic one. What is byte-identical is only the three-word opening the row actually quoted with an ellipsis - so the quoted evidence is clean and the sentence built on it is not. This is a count-object mismatch plus an unqualified verbatim claim, and the antiphonal-unit argument survives once the object is named correctly (the opening formula recurs; the line does not).

challenges.claim: The rationale's 'repeated word-for-word' and the rejected_alternative's 'word-for-word repetition of the gate-command line' are false at every collation tier - MT 24:7 and 24:9 differ in two of nine words - and the 2-verse sweep attached to that claim was measured on the three-word opening formula, not on the line.
evidence: Word-by-word splice of the two MT verses (identity psalm; web:Ps.24.7 = oshb:Ps.24.7, web:Ps.24.9 = oshb:Ps.24.9): word 4 is וְֽ֭הִנָּשְׂאוּ at oshb:Ps.24.7 but וּ֭שְׂאוּ at oshb:Ps.24.9 - niphal against qal imperative, not a spelling variant; word 7 is וְ֝יָב֗וֹא at oshb:Ps.24.7 but וְ֝יָבֹא at oshb:Ps.24.9 (plene against defective). Words 1-3 and 5-6 and 8-9 are byte-identical.
Full-verse tier comparison from consonantal_index.json: oshb:Ps.24.7 and oshb:Ps.24.9 are unequal at byte, at accent_stripped, AND at skeleton - so no tier supports 'word-for-word'.

sweep.py --skel on the first two cola, digit-bearing, unit = verses: the 24:7 line form returns 1 verse book-wide (oshb:Ps.24.7) and the 24:9 line form returns 1 verse book-wide (oshb:Ps.24.9). Each line occurs exactly once; neither is repeated.

sweep.py --skel on the three-word opening שְׂא֤וּ שְׁעָרִ֨ים רָֽאשֵׁיכֶ֗ם returns 2 verses / 2 occurrences book-wide (oshb:Ps.24.7, oshb:Ps.24.9) - this, and only this, is what the row's cited 2-verse figure measures, and it is the correct scope for the antiphony argument.
WEB corroborates the difference the row calls verbatim: “Be lifted up, you everlasting doors” (web:Ps.24.7) against “yes, lift them up, you everlasting doors” (web:Ps.24.9).

reviews.reasoning: Span Ps.25.1-Ps.25.14. Ps 25 is an identity psalm (offset map rule 'identity', 22 = 22), so the row's web:Ps.25.0 = oshb:Ps.25.1 opening form is correct and owner-ruled. All four Hebrew quotes in the device note collate at byte tier. Two of the three acrostic statements check out against both the bytes and psalm_device_inventory.json, whose Ps 25 entry gives first_letters_mt 'aleph aleph gimel dalet he zayin ...' and letters_missing of three letters (bet, waw, qof): the bet-buried claim is exact (oshb:Ps.25.2 word 1 is אֱֽלֹהַ֗י, word 2 is בְּךָ֣), and the waw-skip claim is exact (oshb:Ps.25.5 opens with he, oshb:Ps.25.6 opens with zayin in the quoted form). The third statement is byte-false, and it is the one that describes the row's own opening verse - see OL-062-1. Separately, the seam warrant at 14|15 is register-based and the block it describes does not hold that register throughout - see OL-062-2. The petition-verb cluster claimed for vv. 4-7 does check out in the bytes (imperatives in each of 25:4, 25:5, 25:6, 25:7), and the gnomic shift at v. 8 is real (third-person nominal predication opening oshb:Ps.25.8). 'medium' confidence and the whole-psalm rejected_alternative are honestly calibrated for a psalm whose acrostic runs across the seam.

challenges.claim: The device note's statement that v. 1's own opening word is the aleph word misstates the very MT verse it cites: oshb:Ps.25.1 opens with the superscription word, and the aleph word is its second word - the same positional sense the note applies one clause later to v. 2.
evidence: Byte splice of the whole verse (identity psalm; web:Ps.25.1 = oshb:Ps.25.1): לְדָוִ֡ד אֵלֶ֥יךָ יְ֝הוָ֗ה נַפְשִׁ֥י אֶשָּֽׂא - word 1 is לְדָוִ֡ד and word 2 is אֵלֶ֥יךָ. The note names the word 2 form as the opening word.
The note's own next clause uses 'opening word' and 'second word' positionally for oshb:Ps.25.2 (word 1 אֱֽלֹהַ֗י, word 2 בְּךָ֣), so the positional sense is the note's own, not one I am importing.

psalm_device_inventory.json superscriptions entry for Ps 25 records mt_title_verses 'prefix_of_v1' with label le_david - i.e. the title is a prefix inside MT v1, which is exactly why the aleph word cannot be verse-initial.
The row asserts the same fact in its own boundary_evidence_refs (web:Ps.25.0 = oshb:Ps.25.1, the title pseudo-ref mapping into MT v1), so the device note contradicts the row's own citation.

Materiality: the note is presenting Ps 25's acrostic irregularities, and it renders the aleph line as regular while flagging the bet line as irregular, when in the bytes the acrostic letter is word 2 in both verses.

challenges.claim: The seam warrant 'personal petition resumes at v. 15' does not hold, because the vv. 8-14 block the row characterizes as gnomic description of Yahweh contains an undisclosed direct-address petition at v. 11.
evidence: Byte splice (identity psalm; web:Ps.25.11 = oshb:Ps.25.11): לְמַֽעַן שִׁמְךָ֥ יְהוָ֑ה וְֽסָלַחְתָּ֥ לַ֝עֲוֺנִ֗י כִּ֣י רַב הֽוּא - second-person suffix on the noun 'your name', a 2ms qatal-form verb of pardoning, and a 1cs suffix on 'my iniquity'. This is direct address with a first-person object, not third-person description.
The row's own witness renders it as petition: “For your name’s sake, Yahweh, pardon my iniquity, for it is great.” (web:Ps.25.11).
Contrast the verses the characterization does fit, which are third-person predication about Yahweh: oshb:Ps.25.8 opens טוֹב וְיָשָׁ֥ר יְהוָ֑ה and oshb:Ps.25.14 opens ס֣וֹד יְ֭הוָה.

Effect on the warrant, not on the span: petition does not first 'resume' at v. 15, so the register criterion the row uses to cut at 14|15 is already satisfied inside the block it declines to cut. The span may still be right on other grounds; the stated reason for it is not accurate as written.

reviews.reasoning: Span Ps.25.15-Ps.25.22. All three Hebrew quotes collate at byte tier against their cited refs. The acrostic account is accurate where it is checkable: psalm_device_inventory.json gives Ps 25 a first_letters_mt string carrying resh twice in succession at the v. 18 and v. 19 positions and letters_missing of three letters including qof, which is precisely the doubling the note describes; the tav claim at v. 21 is confirmed by the bytes (oshb:Ps.25.21 opens תֹּם וָיֹ֥שֶׁר); and the supernumerary pe at v. 22 is confirmed both by the quoted byte form and by the inventory string's trailing pe. The uniqueness claim carried by 'the acrostic's one repeated-word doubling' is true, which I verified by listing the line-initial word of all 22 verses from the bytes: only the v. 18 / v. 19 pair repeats. The v. 15 front seam is a genuine tier-1 shift - third-person gnomic predication through v. 14 gives way to first-person declaration at oshb:Ps.25.15 - and the row discloses the rival at v. 16 in its rejected_alternative rather than hiding it, with 'medium' confidence to match. The wait-for-Yahweh echo it draws between v. 21 and v. 3 is real in the Hebrew and not merely an artifact of the English: both carry the same root, as does v. 5. Three observations, none of them defects. The two resh words are the same lexeme but not the same token: v. 18 carries a cantillation accent and v. 19 a meteg, so they are unequal at byte and, because accent-stripping retains meteg, unequal at accent_stripped too, matching only at skeleton - the note displays both pointed forms, so a reader is not misled, and 'the same word' is a lexical claim rather than a verbatim one. 'Completes the standard 22-letter sequence with tav' reads naturally as reaching tav in the alphabet, though the psalm's realized surface sequence is 19 of 22 letters per the inventory. And boundary_evidence_refs holds a single ref that is neither seam, though every seam verse is quoted inline with its own web: ref in the rationale and check_refs_mirror returns GREEN.

Span Ps.26.1-Ps.26.7. The span itself is well warranted and I do not contest it: MT 26:7 closes the purpose clause opened by the ritual action of v. 6 - the verse opens with a lamed-infinitive construct, which is the grammatical fact behind the row's 'purpose clause continues directly' sentence - and MT 26:8 opens verse-initially with the divine name as vocative, a clean tier-1 addressee shift. Ps 26 is an identity psalm (offset map rule 'identity', 12 = 12), so the web:Ps.26.0 = oshb:Ps.26.1 opening form is correct. Both device-note Hebrew quotes collate at byte tier, and the row's rival-seam disclosure at v. 6 with 'medium' confidence is honest calibration. The defect is in the inclusio note's characterization of what those two byte-true quotes share - see OL-064-1. One thing I checked and am not filing: pmarks_Ps.json records a K/Q note at Ps.26.2, inside this span, and the row does not disclose it - but the row quotes only WEB at that verse and never quotes the Hebrew of 26:2, so the disclose-when-quoted rule is not triggered, and citation_sweep and check_marks both return GREEN on the row.

challenges.claim: The inclusio note calls the two integrity clauses at oshb:Ps.26.1 and oshb:Ps.26.11 'the same phrase' when only one word of each recurs, and that word matches only from the accent-stripped tier down while the verbs the note quotes beside it differ at every tier.
evidence: The two quoted spans, spliced byte-true (identity psalm; web:Ps.26.1 = oshb:Ps.26.1, web:Ps.26.11 = oshb:Ps.26.11): בְּתֻמִּ֣י הָלַ֑כְתִּי against בְּתֻמִּ֥י אֵלֵ֗ךְ. They share one word and differ in the other.

Even the shared word is not byte-identical: בְּתֻמִּ֣י at oshb:Ps.26.1 carries U+05A3 where בְּתֻמִּ֥י at oshb:Ps.26.11 carries U+05A5. Byte tier: unequal. accent_stripped: equal. So the recurrence is citable only at accent_stripped or below, and the tier has to be named.
The verbs are different words, not variants: הָלַ֑כְתִּי (suffix-conjugation) against אֵלֵ֗ךְ (prefix-conjugation); unequal at byte, at accent_stripped, and at skeleton.

sweep.py --skel, unit = verses: the 26:1 two-word phrase returns 1 verse book-wide (oshb:Ps.26.1) and the 26:11 two-word phrase returns 1 verse book-wide (oshb:Ps.26.11). A phrase repeated as an inclusio would return 2; each returns 1, which is the direct measurement of the claim's falsity.

The note's own glosses concede the difference by rendering one as completed action and the other as future action, so the phrase-identity wording contradicts the material it is attached to. The inclusio is real at the level of the shared word plus a shared verbal root; it is the verbatim wording that fails, and the repair is a re-description, not a new device.

reviews.reasoning: Span Ps.26.8-Ps.26.12. The front seam is correct and byte-confirmable: oshb:Ps.26.8 opens verse-initially with the divine name, which is the addressee shift the row cites, and the row discloses the v. 9 rival in its rejected_alternative with 'medium' confidence. The dissociation echo it draws between vv. 4-5 and v. 9 is real in the Hebrew and not just in the English: the same preposition governs the company being refused in oshb:Ps.26.4, oshb:Ps.26.5 and oshb:Ps.26.9. Its integrity-vow observation at v. 11 is phrased as recurring language rather than as verbatim repetition, which is the correct strength for what the bytes support. The device note's Hebrew quote collates at byte tier against oshb:Ps.26.12 - but the quote and the gloss attached to it do not cover the same span, which is the defect I file as OL-065-1. One observation, not filed: boundary_evidence_refs holds only the two vv. 4-5 echo refs and neither seam verse, though both seam verses are quoted inline with their own web: refs in the rationale and check_refs_mirror returns GREEN over the cluster.

challenges.claim: In the v. 12 device note the byte-true Hebrew quote and its English gloss cover different spans of oshb:Ps.26.12: the quote opens on a word the gloss drops, and the gloss ends on the divine name, whose bytes lie outside the quote.
evidence: The full verse spliced byte-true (identity psalm; web:Ps.26.12 = oshb:Ps.26.12) is six words: רַ֭גְלִי עָֽמְדָ֣ה בְמִישׁ֑וֹר בְּ֝מַקְהֵלִ֗ים אֲבָרֵ֥ךְ יְהוָֽה.

The note quotes words 3-5, בְמִישׁ֑וֹר בְּ֝מַקְהֵלִ֗ים אֲבָרֵ֥ךְ, but glosses words 4-6, בְּ֝מַקְהֵלִ֗ים אֲבָרֵ֥ךְ יְהוָֽה. Word 3, בְמִישׁ֑וֹר (the 'level ground / even place' term), is inside the quote and absent from the gloss; word 6, יְהוָֽה, is inside the gloss and absent from the quote.

WEB shows the same split across the verse's two clauses, so the mismatch is not a rendering artifact: “My foot stands in an even place. In the congregations I will bless Yahweh.” (web:Ps.26.12) - the gloss reproduces the second clause while the quote begins inside the first.

This is the standing quote-and-gloss parity rule, and the repair is a re-cut rather than a truncation: either extend the quote to word 6 to match the gloss, or drop word 3 from the quote and gloss words 4-6 only.
